full_text_en:
Jingpai Co., Ltd. v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — administrative dispute over trademark refusal review

【Ruling Summary】

According to Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, a mark that is identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China shall not be used as a trademark. The phrase "identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China" as used herein means that the mark as a whole is identical or similar to the national name of China. If the mark contains characters that are identical or similar to the national name of China, but when combined with other elements, as a whole no longer constitutes identity or similarity with the national name of China, it should not be deemed as a mark identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2010) Xing Ti Zi No. 4

Petitioner (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, address: No. 8, Sanlihe East Road, Xicheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Xu Ruibiao, Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Miao Guijuan, Examiner of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.

Agent ad litem: Qiao Xianghui, Examiner of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Jingpai Co., Ltd., address: No. 169, Daye Avenue, Daye City, Hubei Province.

Legal Representative: Wu Shaoxun, Chairman of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Xinxia, Trademark Agent of Beijing Huizhida Intellectual Property Agency Co., Ltd.

Agent ad litem: Sun Kezhi, Intellectual Property Manager of Jingpai Co., Ltd.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board), in a dispute with Jingpai Co., Ltd. over administrative refusal review of a trademark, refused to accept the administrative judgment (2009) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 829 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court on August 19, 2009, and applied to this Court for retrial. Upon review, this Court issued the administrative ruling (2010) Zhi Xing Zi No. 4 on August 6, 2010, deciding to initiate a retrial of this case. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on September 27, 2010. Miao Guijuan and Qiao Xianghui, agents ad litem of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board, and Wang Xinxia, agent ad litem of Jingpai Co., Ltd., appeared in court for the proceedings. This case is now concluded.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court and the Beijing High People's Court found through trial that: On October 20, 2005, Jingpai Co., Ltd. applied to the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Office) for registration of the trademark "China Jinjiu" (Application No. 4953206, hereinafter referred to as the applied-for mark) on goods in Class 33, including fruit wines (containing alcohol), aperitifs, distilled beverages, wine, alcoholic beverages (beverages), rice wine, alcoholic liquids, alcoholic beverages (excluding beer), yellow rice wine, and edible alcohol. On February 26, 2008, the Trademark Office issued the trademark refusal notice ZC4953206BH1, holding that the applied-for mark contained the national name of China, could not be used as a trademark, and was not suitable for registration. In accordance with Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) and Article 28 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law), the registration application for the applied-for mark was rejected. Jingpai Co., Ltd., dissatisfied with the refusal decision, applied to the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board for review, arguing that: The main element "Jin" in the applied-for mark was a trademark already registered by Jingpai Co., Ltd., enjoying high reputation and having been recognized as a well-known trademark. The fonts and presentation styles of "China" and "Jin" in the applied-for mark were different, and "China" merely served to indicate the country of the applicant. According to the Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards, the applied-for mark was not within the scope of prohibited registration, and Jingpai Co., Ltd. requested the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to grant preliminary approval of the applied-for mark. On November 24, 2008, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board issued the Decision on the Refusal Review of Trademark No. 4953206 "China Jinjiu" (Shang Ping Zi [2008] No. 28028, hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 28028), holding that: "China" in the applied-for mark was the national name of China, which belonged to the mark explicitly prohibited from use as a trademark under Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law, and should be rejected according to law. Jingpai Co., Ltd.'s assertion that adding "China" to its relatively well-known trademark could automatically obtain registration lacked legal basis. Therefore, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board decided to reject the registration application for the applied-for mark.

Jingpai Co., Ltd., dissatisfied with Decision No. 28028, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, alleging that: Although the applied-for mark contained the national name of China, the mark as a whole was neither identical nor similar to the national name of China. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board erred in applying Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law and requested the revocation of Decision No. 28028. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found at first instance that: The applied-for mark was a composite mark consisting of the Chinese characters "China Jinjiu" and a square seal design. Among them, the character "Jin" was in running script, with a font different from the other three characters, vigorous in form, prominently protruding to the left of the square seal, and significantly larger than the other three characters, making it the distinctive part of the applied-for mark. The three characters "China Wine" in the square seal design had a font clearly distinct from "Jin." Although they contained the national name of China, that part was more likely to be understood by consumers as indicating the country of the trademark applicant. Decision No. 28028, issued by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board, merely based on the fact that "China" in the applied-for mark was the national name of China, deemed the applied-for mark as a mark prohibited from use as a trademark under Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law, with insufficient evidence. On April 7, 2009, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered the administrative judgment (2009) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 441, and in accordance with Article 54, Paragraph (2), Sub-item 1 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, decided to revoke Decision No. 28028. The case acceptance fee of RMB 100 was to be borne by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. The Beijing High People's Court found at second instance that: Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law provides that marks identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China shall not be used as trademarks. The above legal provision indicates that, in general, marks identical or similar to the national name of China are prohibited from use as trademarks, except where the applied-for mark contains the national name of China, but the national name is independent of other distinctive elements and merely serves to indicate the country of the applicant. In this case, the applied-for mark was a composite mark consisting of the Chinese characters "China Jinjiu" and a square seal design. Among them, the character "Jin" was in running script, with a font different from the other three characters, vigorous in form, prominently protruding to the left of the square seal, and significantly larger than the other three characters, making it the distinctive part of the applied-for mark. The three characters "China Wine" in the square seal design had a font clearly distinct from "Jin." Although they contained the national name of China, that part was more likely to be understood by consumers as merely indicating the country of the trademark applicant. Therefore, Decision No. 28028 issued by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board had unclear findings of fact and insufficient evidence. The first-instance court correctly revoked it, and the decision should be upheld. On August 19, 2009, the Beijing High People's Court rendered the administrative judgment (2009) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 829, upholding the first-instance judgment, with the second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 borne by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board applied for retrial, alleging that: Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law provides that "marks identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China shall not be used as trademarks." The Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards clearly state that if a mark contains characters identical or similar to the national name of China, it should be determined as identical or similar to the national name of China. The Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards provide three exceptions; beyond these, marks containing the national name of China are uniformly not registered and are prohibited from use. The strict provisions on the registrability of marks containing the national name of China are due to the following reasons: First, the provisions of the Trademark Law on trademark registration management not only protect the interests of trademark registrants but also bear the responsibility of safeguarding national dignity, protecting consumer rights, and maintaining social public interests and the socialist market economic order. The national name of the People's Republic of China (including its abbreviation), together with the national flag and national emblem, are national symbols closely linked to national dignity. To ensure that market entities use the national name appropriately and legitimately, and to avoid possible abuse of national symbols in commercial use, strict examination of trademarks containing the national name has always been carried out, and it has become an examination practice to generally prohibit the registration of trademarks bearing the national name. Second, the combination of "China" and other distinctive marks is easily identified as an abbreviation of an enterprise name. However, China's regulations on enterprise name registration management impose strict conditions on enterprises using "China" in their names. In the examination of trademark registrability, consideration should also be given to the restrictive provisions in enterprise name laws and regulations, to avoid enterprise names that do not meet registration conditions from appearing in the form of trademarks. In this case, the applied-for mark contained the characters "China," forming a visual whole, with "China" becoming an inseparable part of the mark. It did not fall within the situation referred to in the Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards where the national name is independent of other distinctive elements and merely serves to indicate the country of the applicant. The applicant for registration of the applied-for mark was "Jingpai Co., Ltd.," which was not a company eligible to use the word "China." Combining "China" with the enterprise name in the trademark constituted improper use of the national name of China. The original courts failed to carefully consider the special nature of trademarks containing the national name of China, and the rendered judgment might lead to unrestricted registration and use of the national name by different categories of market entities. To avoid a large number of trademark registrations containing "China" that might cause abuse of the national name of China, and to maintain a good trademark registration management order, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board requested the revocation of the first-instance and second-instance judgments and the upholding of Decision No. 28028 issued by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board.

Jingpai Co., Ltd. argued in its defense that: The Trademark Law does not take the enterprise name registration management regulations as the legal basis for regulating trademark registration, nor does it divide applicants for trademark registration into different categories. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's practice of allowing some entities to register trademarks containing "China" while restricting others violated the principles of equality and uniformity of the legal system. Although the applied-for mark contained the national name, the mark as a whole was neither identical nor similar to the national name of China. The mere inclusion of the national name in the applied-for mark should not be deemed as similarity to the national name. In practice, many trademarks containing "China" have been registered. The Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards explicitly provide that "where a mark applied for by a Chinese applicant contains the national name of China and the national name is independent of other distinctive elements and merely serves to indicate the country of the applicant," registration is permitted. In the applied-for mark, the distinctive element was the cursive "Jin," while "China" and "Wine" were in common presentation forms, with the national name independent of the distinctive element and merely indicating the country of the applicant. Therefore, the applied-for mark fully complied with the Trademark Examination and Adjudication Standards and should be registered. The applied-for mark had been used for many years, received multiple honors, and gained consumer recognition, with no evidence showing that it harmed national sovereignty or dignity. In summary, Jingpai Co., Ltd. requested the upholding of the administrative judgment (2009) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 829.

This Court confirmed the facts found by the original courts. During the retrial, Jingpai Co., Ltd. submitted evidence including customs export declarations, sales contracts, advertising videos, design patent certificate for Jinjiu, and honorary certificates showing that "China Jinjiu" won the title of Consumer Satisfaction Product of Hubei Province for the periods 1999-2000 and 2001-2002, aiming to prove that Jingpai Co., Ltd. had extensively used the applied-for mark and received multiple honors and consumer recognition. Additionally, Jingpai Co., Ltd. submitted evidence of the registration information for trademark No. 5654179 "China Phoenix" of Phoenix Technology Group Co., Ltd., to show that entities without "China" in their enterprise names could register trademarks containing the characters "China."

This Court found in retrial that a trademark is a mark used to distinguish goods or services provided by different producers or operators. Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law provides that marks identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China shall not be used as trademarks. The phrase "identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China" as used herein means that the mark as a whole is identical or similar to the national name of China. If the mark contains characters that are identical or similar to the national name of China, but when combined with other elements, as a whole no longer constitutes identity or similarity with the national name of China, it should not be deemed as a mark identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China. In this case, the applied-for mark can be clearly identified as consisting of three parts: "China," "Jin," and "Wine." Although it contains the national name "China," as a whole it is not identical or similar to the national name of China. Therefore, the applied-for mark does not constitute a mark identical or similar to the national name of the People's Republic of China. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's determination that the applied-for mark fell under Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law as a mark similar to the national name of China, and its consequent rejection of the registration application, was inappropriate. This Court hereby corrects that determination, and the related retrial grounds are not supported.

However, the national name is a symbol of the state. If it were allowed to be arbitrarily included as a component of a trademark and used commercially, it would lead to abuse of the national name, damage national dignity, and may also have other negative impacts on social public interests and public order. Therefore, for marks containing characters identical or similar to the national name of China, although their registration applications should not be examined under Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Trademark Law, it does not mean that they are registrable or usable as trademarks; they should still be examined under other relevant provisions of the Trademark Law. For example, if such a mark has adverse effects, it may still be deemed as a trademark that cannot be used or registered in accordance with the Trademark Law. Accordingly, in this case, the reasoning of the first-instance and second-instance judgments of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court and the Beijing High People's Court was inappropriate and should be corrected, but the conclusion to revoke Decision No. 28028 was correct and should be upheld. In this case, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board still needs to examine whether the applied-for mark violates other relevant provisions of the Trademark Law, and therefore it is necessary to order the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to make a new review decision.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 54, Paragraph (2), Sub-item 2, and Article 63, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 76, Paragraph 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. Affirm the administrative judgment (2009) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 829 of the Beijing High People's Court;

2. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce shall make a new review decision.

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 and the second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100, totaling RMB 200, shall be borne by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge Xia Junli

Acting Judge Wang Yanfang

Acting Judge Zhou Yunchuan

December 24, 2010

Clerk Zhang Bo

[Profile of the Presiding Judge]

Xia Junli, Senior Judge: Born in 1968, Master of Laws. Appointed as judge of the Supreme People's Court in 2009.
